transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-10-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Walker (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Martin Reyes (Verdigris CTO), Li Wei (Verdigris Lead ML Eng), Sofia Alvarez (Verdigris PM)

Summary: quick walkthrough of schema-first action chaining, how Redwood Console surfaces tool invocations, pilot scope.

00:00 Ethan Walker: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes. Quick intros?
00:06 Martin Reyes: Hi I'm Martin, CTO at Verdigris, mainly focused on reliability and integration with our NMS.
00:11 Li Wei: Li, lead ML, looking at automating ticket triage and some network config helper tools, low latency matters.
00:18 Sofia Alvarez: Sofia, PM, goal is to reduce mean time to resolution and automate routine config tasks.
00:24 Ethan: Awesome. Priya's gonna walk through JSON mode, action chaining, and we'll show Console + Optimize hints. Priya?
00:31 Priya Nair: Hey! So first slide — schema enforcement. The idea is you define a typed response contract, we validate at runtime and reject or map outputs. In practice you get a JSON schema like {"action": "string","params": {"device_id":"string","cmd":"string"}} — we run the model, then the runtime validates before invoking your tool. (transcription: sometimes schema examples mangled in the recording)
01:05 Martin: How strict is validation? If model returns slightly different keys do you try to map or fail the request?
01:12 Priya: Good q — we support three modes: strict (fail), tolerant (attempt normalization heuristics), and patched (automated repair with a small LLM pass). You choose per-route. For pilots we usually run tolerant with a repair policy off by default.
01:28 Li: For chaining, we need to call the ticketing API, then maybe call a push-config tool — what guarantees do you provide about ordering and idempotency?
01:38 Priya: Two patterns: orchestrated chains where Console runs a sequencer with explicit step states persisted to the KV cache, or self-contained chains where the model returns a list of actions and Redwood calls them in order. For idempotency, you can provide a dedupe-key in the schema. We also persist a lightweight execution log with each step to support rollback/fallback.
02:05 Martin: When you say KV cache — is that per-customer? data residency concerns.
02:10 Priya: Yes it's per-tenant and can be colocated in your VPC with Redwood Private. We encrypt at rest with KMS and you can integrate with your HSM. Small note: our transcript sometimes says KV "cash" in auto-text.
02:23 Ethan: Security quick note — we support SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs shipped to your SIEM, SOC 2 compliance. For Verdigris we recommended Private or Dedicated for initial pilot because of PCI-adjacent telecom configs.
02:40 Sofia: Ok good. On latency: we need median 200ms per user-visible op, is that realistic with JSON validation + tool calls?
02:48 Priya: Depends. If model needs to synthesize a ticket ID and you make an external API call, that adds network latency. For purely in-memory chaining we can stay sub-200ms for generation on dedicated capacity with batching tuned via Redwood Optimize. For hybrid flows we recommend prefix caching of prompts and pre-populating the KV with device metadata.
03:15 Li: Any suggestions on model variants? We're cost-sensitive.
03:19 Priya: Yes — use a faster cheaper model for routine triage, route escalations to a higher-quality variant. Redwood supports automated fallback policies in the routing layer. Optimize will recommend quantization profiles; for example q5_0 gives 2–3x speed up for triage workloads while retaining acceptable quality.
03:40 Martin: Demo time?
03:42 Priya: Yeah switching to the Console. (screen-sharing noise)
03:46 Priya: Here is the route configuration — you can pin schema, set the validation mode, and define tool bindings. I'm showing a ticket-triage route. Note: schema examples are abbreviated in the clip, but the repo link is in the notes: https://redwood.ai/console/schemas/verdigris-starter
04:10 Ethan: We're also going to show a live chain. Model suggests action: create_ticket -> call-ticket-api -> run-diagnosis -> call-config-push. Console shows each tool invocation and the raw payload plus validated JSON.
04:30 Li: I'm seeing a mismatch: the model returned 'deviceId' camelCase but our API expects snake_case.
04:36 Priya: Yep that's where the tolerant repair mode normalized keys. On the backend the transformer did a quick key map. You can also define mapping rules in the schema.
05:05 Sofia: What about partial failures? If call-config-push fails, do you have automatic rollbacks?
05:12 Priya: We have retry policies and a step-level failure handler. For transactional semantics you can mark steps as compensating and provide an idempotent reversal action. We log the state and expose manual retry controls in the Console.
05:40 Martin: Audit logs — can they be sent to our Splunk instance?
05:44 Ethan: Yes, audit logs can stream via HTTPS/Kinesis/Syslog, or be written to a VPC endpoint you control. We also provide field-level redaction configs for PII.
06:05 Li: For the tool calls, how do you handle credentials? Do Redwood handle secrets?
06:10 Priya: For Redwood Private, secrets live in your KMS and we only refer to them by reference in the config. For hosted mode we use our vault with optional customer-managed keys. We'll share the security whitepaper after the call.
06:26 Martin: On observability, can we see per-step latency and token counts?
06:30 Priya: Yep Console exposes per-route per-step telemetry — token breakdown, model latency, tool call latency. Optimize provides recommendations to change batch sizes or switch kernel selection for your workload distribution.
06:52 Ethan: Quick interruption, a question from earlier — scaling: what happens under heavy load and how do you ensure cost predictability?
06:58 Priya: You can reserve Dedicated pools or use burst policies. We recommend a canary route for high-volume traffic and an automated fallback to a cheaper model or even a rule-based fallback for certain intents.
07:18 Li: How easy is local testing? We want to run unit tests for schemas.
07:22 Priya: Console has a 'sandbox runner' where you upload sample prompts and it simulates the chain including tool stubs. That helps generate integration tests and a golden output set for regression detection.
07:40 Sofia: Can we assert correctness on the model's outputs? like we want tickets created only when severity >= 3.
07:47 Priya: You define such guardrails in the policy layer: route conditions and pre-invoke assertions. If assertion fails, the model is asked to re-run with more constrained instruction or we fall back to manual review.
08:10 Martin: About the pilot — we need to quantify success. Proposed: 4-week pilot, ingest 1k daily prompts, aim for 60% automation rate and maintain median RT < 300ms for triage flows. Thoughts?
08:22 Ethan: Sounds reasonable. We'll scope the pilot: console sandbox, data ingestion, run 1k prompts/day synthetic and real, Optimize tuning pass at week 2.
08:30 Li: What about data retention and logging — we need logs for 12 months for audits.
08:34 Ethan: For Private deployments you manage retention policy; for hosted we offer configurable retention windows and export hooks. We'll provide an export of logs to your archival bucket.
08:50 Priya: Back to the demo — walking through a fault scenario where a tool returns 503. Console surfaced the error, the sequencer retried with exponential backoff and then switched to manual-queue step.
09:05 Martin: Is there a way to replay a chain for debugging?
09:09 Priya: Yes — replay tool reconstructs the prompt + KV state. Note: replay uses sanitized logs to avoid leaking secrets.
09:20 Li: Any gotchas with rate limits? Our NMS may be chatty.
09:24 Priya: We have per-route rate limits, and you can configure backpressure and throttling. For pilot we recommend conservative rate limits with auto-escalation thresholds.
09:38 Ethan: Quick mention of integrations — we have prebuilt connectors to ServiceNow, Jira, Slack, and custom webhook integrations.
09:50 Sofia: For the initial schema, could you show a starter template for ticket triage?
09:54 Priya: sure — showing schema. (reads) action: ENUM[create_ticket, add_context, escalate, no_action]; params: object with device_id, severity:int, summary:string. We'll send the full template.
10:20 Martin: Regarding function calling vs Redwood's tool binding, are they different?
10:25 Priya: Function calling is model-native: model returns a call spec and we execute. Redwood tool bindings give you more control: middleware, validation, retries, RBAC; they run inside the sequencer and are declarative in the route config.
10:46 Li: For chained calls, do you serialize state between steps so a later model call can see previous step outputs?
10:50 Priya: Yes — step outputs are stored and optionally injected into later prompts. We support intelligent windowing so only relevant context is rehydrated to avoid token bloat.
11:12 Martin: Suppose we need to run an external diagnostic that takes 30s, how does the flow behave?
11:17 Priya: You can execute async steps: we return an interim status to the user and continue, or mark the route as long-polling. Console has a UI for async completions.
11:30 Sofia: Any mention of fallback to human-in-the-loop?
11:33 Priya: Yes, route configs support human review gates. If model confidence is low or assertions fail, we escalate to the ops queue.
11:46 Ethan: Ok let's talk onboarding and timelines for the 4-week pilot.
11:50 Ethan: Week 0: account setup and sandbox. Week 1: ingest sample prompts + define schemas. Week 2: run synthetic load and Optimize tuning. Week 3: iterate on guardrails and integrate with ticketing. Week 4: review and handoff.
12:15 Li: Do you need any network peering for Private?
12:18 Ethan: For Private we set up VPC peering or PrivateLink. We'll share the network checklist.
12:25 Martin: Cost model question — for the pilot, how do we estimate tokens and tool invocation costs?
12:31 Priya: We'll provide a cost worksheet. Optimize will also simulate per-token spend and batching effects. For action-heavy flows, tool calls are often the majority of cost due to external API use rather than model tokens.
12:52 Sofia: Any compliance docs we can share now?
12:55 Ethan: Yes, I'll attach SOC2 + encryption + data flow diagrams. Priya will add the security whitepaper.
13:10 Martin: Sounds good. A couple of housekeeping items: we will need a statement of work for the pilot and an NDA in place before exchanging PII samples.
13:20 Ethan: We'll circulate SOW + NDA; target to have both signed by 2026-10-05.
13:30 Priya: Final live note: Console shows a visual run of the chain — you can click each step to expand payloads and see validation diffs.
13:40 Sofia: Great. That is super helpful.
13:45 Ethan: Alright time check — 45 minutes. Let's recap next steps.

Recap / Next Steps
- Ethan to send pilot pricing and PO template (due 2026-10-04)
- Priya to provision Console sandbox and send schema starter templates + sandbox link (due 2026-10-03)
- Verdigris (Li) to upload representative prompt set and latency/SLA targets (due 2026-10-07)
- Legal: SOW + NDA to be circulated and signed (due 2026-10-05)

Notes: Links shared during call: https://redwood.ai/console/schemas/verdigris-starter, https://redwood.ai/docs/security-whitepaper

End of transcript
